features.headline: Best friends Pat Surtain II, Jaylen Waddle ecstatic about reuniting on Broncos
features.desc: Surtain and Waddle bonded immediately at Alabama six years ago and have embraced the chance to play together again in Denver on a team with Super Bowl hopes.
body: ENGLEWOOD, Colo. — Karl Scott still laughs at the memory, the moment when he knew Denver Broncos cornerback Pat Surtain II and wide receiver Jaylen Waddle were destined to be best friends.

It was at a Tuscaloosa, Alabama, bowling alley on a blistering summer afternoon in 2018 during what Scott, who was the Alabama defensive backs coach at the time, described as a team-building event for the Crimson Tide's incoming recruiting class.
Surtain and Waddle were among Alabama's newly minted freshmen, and their bond already stood out to the coach.

"They weren't going to be just guys who happened to be on the same team. They were going to be the guy who's got your back for each other," said Scott, now the Seattle Seahawks' secondary coach and defensive passing game coordinator.
"Frick and Frack, man, just Frick and Frack. There wasn't a time I didn't see them together."
A wide smile crept across Surtain's face after a recent Broncos practice when recalling that day, with the All-Pro calling it "just the beginning of it all."

The Broncos are nearly two-thirds through the 2026 season, the first that Waddle and Surtain have spent as teammates since playing together on Alabama's 2020 College Football Playoff championship team.
They were reunited when the Broncos acquired Waddle from the Miami Dolphins this past offseason for first- and third-round draft picks along with a fourth-round pick swap.

And when the 8-2 Broncos play at the 6-4 Pittsburgh Steelers on Friday in Acrisure Stadium (3 p.m. ET, Prime Video), it will be the sixth time Surtain and Waddle have taken the field together not only as NFL teammates, but also close friends.

features.headline: Why Walker Kessler is the X factor for Luka Doncic and the Lakers this season
features.desc: Doncic's first request when he became a Laker? Get an 'A-list' big man. It took a year, but Kessler is that man in Los Angeles.
body: EVEN INSIDE a busy hotel lobby, one with 30-foot ceilings, a gilded life-sized horse statue, a jungle-gym-looking apparatus covering the bar area and an oversized, magenta, metallic art installation at the front entrance, Los Angeles Lakers center Walker Kessler stands out.

Dressed in a gray sweatsuit and a black trucker-style baseball cap on an off night in Birmingham, Michigan, Daxton Hotel patrons turn as the 7-foot-2 Kessler walks from the elevator banks to a seat at a four-top table as L.A.'s new man in the middle.

"It's the way I'm supposed to be," Kessler told ESPN about his height, which puts him as one of the top 10 tallest players in the NBA. "It's weird for me if my feet didn't hang over the bed — that would feel uncomfortable with me."

He has looked mighty comfortable right from the start this season, scoring 26 points on 12-for-12 shooting (including 10 dunks), with nine rebounds and two blocks in his Lakers debut in an opening-night rout over Stephen Curry and the Golden State Warriors.
After the game, he joined the "Inside the NBA" crew and received a stamp of approval from a legendary Lakers center.

"The way you played tonight, you played like the best big man in the league," Shaquille O'Neal told Kessler, who became the first Lakers player since Wilt Chamberlain in 1969 to have that many makes without a miss. "Welcome to the big man alliance."
Just before the segment finished, O'Neal chimed in again.
"I got a new nickname for you," he said. "Your new nickname is, 'Milk Chamberlain.' I love you, Milk."

features.headline: Why the Seahawks are turning back to quarterback Sam Darnold vs. the 49ers
features.desc: Drew Lock has been 'fantastic' filling in for Darnold, who has struggled with injuries but is on track to face 9-1 San Francisco on Sunday.
body: RENTON, Wash. — Having coached Ben Roethlisberger and the Pittsburgh Steelers to a Super Bowl title 18 years ago, Mike Tomlin was speaking from experience when he weighed in on the Seattle Seahawks' quarterback situation.

Hours after backup Drew Lock led Seattle to a 21-13 win over the Las Vegas Raiders on Nov. 15 — his fourth victory in as many fill-in appearances this season — Tomlin correctly predicted during the "Sunday Night Football"
broadcast that coach Mike Macdonald would turn back to beleaguered starter Sam Darnold after the Seahawks' bye.

Tomlin said the Seahawks coach and quarterback were "tied together for life," and that if he were in Macdonald's shoes, he'd stick with Darnold "because of the emotional bank account" he built last season while helping Seattle win Super Bowl LX.
"I think he's spot on," Macdonald said the next day after hearing the Tomlin clip on his Seattle Sports 710-AM radio show.

That helps explain why Darnold — who was a full participant in practice Wednesday and Thursday — will be back in the starting lineup Sunday when Seattle (6-4) faces the NFC West-leading San Francisco 49ers (9-1) at Levi's Stadium in a game the Seahawks must win to keep any hope of staying in the division race alive.
As predictable as Macdonald's decision might have been, it hardly seemed straightforward.

features.headline: Would any USMNT players really make Man United better if they followed Poch?
features.desc: Now that USMNT manager Mauricio Pochettino has taken over Man United, would it make sense for USMNT players to join their ex-coach?
body: If you follow the U.S. men's national team, here's a good sanity check: Imagine going back in time — say, 15 years — and telling your past self about the current situation.

"Yeah, so there's this guy who came up through the FC Dallas academy, moved to Schalke when he was a kid, started for them as an 18-year-old when they finished second in the Bundesliga behind Bayern Munich, and then moved to Juventus.
He has played more Serie A matches for Juve than anyone else in the seven seasons since he joined the team."

"And he just did this news conference where he said, 'Guys from here being talked about going to Manchester United' was 'inevitable.' Oh, and this is important: he was saying that because Manchester United just poached the USMNT manager in the middle of the Premier League season."

Think about all the assumptions your 15-years-younger self would be making, whenever they had regained consciousness after suffering the double-whammy of learning that time travel exists and that the USMNT was one step below Manchester United in the global pecking order.
... Schalke are one of the best development clubs in the world, and Juventus are one of the best clubs in the world, so one of the best soccer players in the world plays for the USMNT now?

And then, well, the USMNT coach is now coaching Manchester United, which might be the best club in the world. If my math is right, then there was a World Cup a couple of months ago — in summer 2026 — so... wait... did the U.S. just win the World Cup?

features.headline: Which NBA players have the most triple-doubles of all time?
features.desc: Russell Westbrook holds the NBA record for most triple-doubles in a career. See who else joins him on the list.
body: Russell Westbrook has more than earned the nickname Mr. Triple Double.
In basketball, a triple-double is when a player compiles a double-digit total in three of five statistical categories (assists, blocks, points, rebounds and steals) over the course of a game.
Blocks and steals were officially recorded by the NBA starting in the 1973-74 season. No player in NBA history has recorded more triple-doubles than Westbrook.
On May 10, 2021, Westbrook became the NBA's career leader in triple-doubles, tallying 28 points, 13 rebounds and 21 assists for the Washington Wizards in a 125-124 loss against the Atlanta Hawks.
It marked the 182nd triple-double of Westbrook's career, passing Oscar Robertson for the most on the all-time list.
Nikola Jokić also has since passed Robertson, whose record stood for more than 47 years.
Westbrook had already broken Robertson's record for the most triple-doubles in a single NBA season (41), recording 42 during the 2016-17 campaign.
